title: Danish Oil
description: Danish oil is a blend of oil and varnish that wipes on easily and gives wood a warm, natural, low-sheen look while adding more protection than pure oil alone. It soaks into the grain on the first coat and builds a thin film on later coats, which makes it forgiving for beginners and easy to repair: a worn spot is simply wiped with another coat. Danish oil suits tabletops that see light use, shelves, and boxes, but it is not as waterproof as polyurethane and needs re-oiling every year or two on hard-used surfaces.

title: Tung Oil
description: Tung oil is pressed from the seeds of the tung tree and gives a hard, water-resistant, matte finish that is prized for fine furniture and wooden boats. Pure tung oil needs many thin coats, often five or more, and each coat needs a full day to cure, so it rewards patience with a deep, natural look that never looks plastic. Tung oil must be pure, not a blend labeled tung oil finish, if the full water resistance is wanted, and it should be thinned with citrus solvent or mineral spirits for the first coats so it soaks in.

title: Linseed Oil
description: Linseed oil is pressed from flaxseed and is the oldest wood finish in common use, giving a warm amber tone that deepens with age. Boiled linseed oil, which contains drying agents, cures in about a day per coat, while raw linseed oil takes much longer and is used mainly where a very slow cure is acceptable. Linseed oil offers only modest protection against water and wear, so it suits tool handles, workbench tops, and rustic pieces that are easy to re-oil, and it is never used alone on a kitchen table that sees spills.

title: Shellac
description: Shellac is a natural resin secreted by the lac insect, dissolved in alcohol, and it is the classic French-polish finish: warm, clear, and fast-drying, with a depth that synthetic finishes struggle to match. Shellac dries in under an hour, seals in odors and stains, and is easily repaired, since a new coat melts into the old one. Its weakness is water and alcohol: a wet glass leaves a white ring and spilled spirits dissolve it, so shellac suits display furniture, boxes, and musical instruments rather than kitchen tables. Shellac is sold by cut, meaning pounds of resin per gallon of alcohol, with a 2-pound cut as the common working strength.

title: Polyurethane (Wipe-On)
description: Wipe-on polyurethane is ordinary polyurethane thinned to wiping consistency, and it is the easiest way for a beginner to get a durable, even film finish without brush marks or drips. Each coat is thin, so four to six coats are normal, but each coat wipes on in minutes and dries in a few hours. Wipe-on polyurethane gives the same water and wear resistance as brush-on polyurethane once enough coats are built, and it suits tabletops, shelves, and boxes. Work in a dust-free space, since dust in a wet coat is the main enemy of a smooth result.

title: Polyurethane (Brush-On)
description: Brush-on polyurethane builds a thick, tough film in two to three coats and is the standard durable finish for floors, tabletops, and kitchen cabinets. It is applied with a high-quality synthetic brush in long, even strokes, and it must not be over-brushed, because working the finish after it starts to tack leaves brush marks and bubbles. Oil-based polyurethane ambers over time and smells strongly while curing, while water-based polyurethane stays clear, dries faster, and cleans up with water. Either way, the surface must be dust-free and the coats thin, since thick coats trap bubbles and take far longer to cure.

title: Lacquer
description: Lacquer is a fast-drying finish sprayed in thin coats that melt into each other, giving a hard, clear, professional-looking film that is the standard finish for production furniture and musical instruments. Lacquer dries to the touch in about 30 minutes and can be recoated without sanding between coats, but it must be sprayed, since brushing lacquer leaves lap marks, and spraying demands a respirator, ventilation, and a spray area away from ignition sources, because lacquer fumes are flammable. Lacquer is damaged by some solvents and by prolonged water contact, so it suits display furniture and instruments rather than wet environments.

title: Varnish
description: Varnish is a traditional resin-and-oil finish that builds a hard, glossy, water-resistant film, and it remains the right choice for boats, bar tops, and any surface that sees standing water. Spar varnish, the outdoor kind, stays flexible so it moves with the wood outdoors instead of cracking, while interior varnish dries harder and is used for floors and furniture. Varnish is brushed on in thin coats and needs a dust-free space and long drying times, often a full day between coats, so it is slower than polyurethane but more forgiving on a surface that must flex.

title: Wood Stain
description: Wood stain is a colorant, not a protective finish on its own: it colors the wood and must be sealed with oil, shellac, or polyurethane afterward, or the color will wear away and stain hands and cloth. Oil stains give even color and long open time, gel stains sit on the surface and suit blotch-prone woods like pine and cherry, and water-based stains dry fast and raise the grain slightly. Stain color always depends on the wood species, so a test board from the same wood is essential before staining the real piece. Stain rags carry the same fire risk as oil rags when the stain is oil-based.

title: Whitewash
description: Whitewash is a thinned white paint or lime wash that lightens wood while letting the grain show through, giving a coastal, rustic look that suits pine, cedar, and reclaimed boards. The classic mix is white latex paint thinned about half and half with water, wiped on and wiped off until the desired lightness is reached. Whitewash must be sealed with a clear topcoat, usually matte polyurethane or wax, or it will rub off and pick up dirt. Whitewash is a color treatment, not a protective finish, and it works best on open-grained woods where the grain pattern stays visible.

title: Milk Paint
description: Milk paint is an old finish made from milk protein, lime, and pigment, and it gives a flat, chalky, historic look with a depth that modern latex paint does not match. It is sold as a powder and mixed with water, it bonds to raw wood without primer, and it can be distressed easily for an antique look by sanding through edges after it dries. Milk paint must be sealed with oil, wax, or polyurethane, since unsealed milk paint is porous and marks easily. Because it is mixed fresh, mixed milk paint keeps only a day or two and must be used promptly.

title: Chalk Paint
description: Chalk paint is a thick, matte decorative paint that sticks to wood with little or no sanding or priming, which makes it popular for refinishing furniture quickly. It dries fast, sands easily for distressing, and must be sealed with wax or a clear topcoat, because unsealed chalk paint is soft and marks with the slightest touch. Chalk paint suits painted furniture, cabinets, and decorative pieces, and it is not a durable finish for tabletops or floors even when sealed. title: Beeswax Finish
description: Beeswax finish is a paste of beeswax and a solvent or oil that is rubbed into wood to give a soft, warm, matte sheen and a pleasant smell. It protects lightly against moisture and handling marks, but it is the softest finish in this guide: it wears away under heavy use, melts in heat, and must be reapplied every few months on hard-used surfaces. Beeswax is ideal for turned bowls, boxes, and decorative pieces, and it is the traditional sealer over milk paint and chalk paint. Beeswax paste is applied with a cloth, left to haze, and buffed to a soft shine.

title: Hardwax Oil
description: Hardwax oil is a modern blend of oils and waxes that soaks into wood like oil and cures to a hard, water-resistant surface like a film finish, which makes it the standard finish for wood floors and countertops. It is applied in two coats, the first soaking in and the second building the surface, and it is repaired easily by spot-applying more oil to a worn area. Hardwax oil needs good ventilation while curing and a full cure of about a week before rugs or heavy use. As with all oil finishes, used application rags must be dried flat outdoors or stored in water, since they can catch fire on their own.

title: Epoxy Topcoat Basics
description: Epoxy topcoat is a two-part resin that cures to a thick, glass-clear, highly waterproof film, and it is used for river tables, bar tops, and countertops where a deep, glossy, waterproof surface is wanted. Epoxy is mixed by exact ratio, usually 1 to 1 or 2 to 1 by volume depending on the product, poured in thin layers to avoid trapped heat and bubbles, and it must be applied in a dust-free space, since every dust speck is trapped forever in the clear film. Epoxy resin and hardener are skin sensitizers, so gloves are mandatory, ventilation is required, and uncured epoxy is never poured down a drain. Epoxy yellows slowly in sunlight unless a UV-stable product is used.

title: Outdoor Spar Finish
description: Outdoor spar finish, also called spar varnish or marine varnish, is a flexible, UV-resistant varnish made for wood that lives outdoors, where sun and rain would crack a hard indoor finish. It contains UV absorbers and stays elastic so it moves with the wood through wet and dry seasons, and it needs recoating every one to two years outdoors, since even the best spar finish wears under sun. Spar finish is brushed on in thin coats, needs a dust-free drying space, and must be applied over dry wood, since trapped moisture under a spar film causes peeling. Spar finish is never used indoors as a substitute for polyurethane, since it stays softer and cures slower.
